question: Walk through the agent design-pattern catalog and when to use each pattern.
directAnswer: The common catalog of agentic patterns is prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, and evaluator-optimizer, plus the fully autonomous agent loop. Prompt chaining fits tasks that decompose into fixed ordered steps. Routing fits tasks where different inputs need different specialized handling. Parallelization fits work that can be split into independent subtasks run at once, or the same task run several times for voting. Orchestrator-workers fits tasks where a central model must dynamically break work into subtasks and delegate them. Evaluator-optimizer fits tasks that benefit from iterative critique and refinement. You choose the simplest pattern that meets the need, escalating to autonomy only when fixed workflows cannot cope.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: These are composable workflow shapes. Chaining is a pipeline; routing is a classifier that dispatches to branches; parallelization runs branches concurrently and aggregates; orchestrator-workers is a coordinator that spawns and combines subtasks it decides at runtime; evaluator-optimizer is a generate-then-critique loop. Autonomous agents let the model drive the whole flow with tools.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A single monolithic prompt handles only so much before quality drops, and different tasks have different structures. The catalog exists to give named, well-understood building blocks so you can match the shape of the workflow to the shape of the problem, and combine them, instead of reinventing control flow each time.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Chaining, routing, and parallelization have developer-defined control flow, so they are predictable. Orchestrator-workers differs from parallelization because the orchestrator decides the subtasks dynamically rather than following a fixed split. Evaluator-optimizer loops a generator and an evaluator until quality is acceptable. Autonomous agents hand control flow to the model itself, using tools in a loop, which is the most flexible but least predictable.

whyImportant: This catalog is the shared vocabulary of agent orchestration, and interviewers use it to test whether you can reason about design rather than just call an API. Being able to map a concrete problem to the right pattern, and justify not using a heavier one, demonstrates real judgment. It underpins nearly every system-design discussion in this field.
realWorldExample: A document-processing product uses several patterns together: routing classifies each incoming document type, chaining runs the extraction pipeline for a given type, parallelization extracts multiple independent fields at once, and evaluator-optimizer refines a generated summary until it passes a quality check. Only the genuinely open-ended research feature uses a fully autonomous agent, keeping the rest of the system on predictable, structured patterns.

nestedTopics.title: Parallelization: sectioning and voting
nestedTopics.explanation: Parallelization takes two forms. Sectioning splits a task into independent subtasks run concurrently and then aggregated, which saves latency. Voting runs the same task multiple times and combines the results, for example by majority, to improve reliability on tasks where multiple attempts catch different errors.

nestedTopics.title: Orchestrator-workers versus parallelization
nestedTopics.explanation: In parallelization the developer fixes how the task is split. In orchestrator-workers a central model decides the subtasks at runtime based on the input, delegates each to a worker, and synthesizes the results. Use orchestrator-workers when you cannot predict the subtasks in advance, such as editing an unknown number of files.

nestedTopics.title: Evaluator-optimizer loops
nestedTopics.explanation: One model generates a candidate and another evaluates it against criteria, feeding critique back for revision, repeating until the output passes. This suits tasks with clear evaluation criteria and where iteration measurably improves quality, like refining a translation or tightening a piece of writing.

followUps.question: How do you decide between a fixed workflow pattern and an autonomous agent?
followUps.answer: You choose a fixed workflow, meaning chaining, routing, parallelization, or a predefined orchestration, whenever you can enumerate the steps or branches in advance, because fixed flows are more predictable, cheaper, easier to test, and easier to debug. You choose an autonomous agent, where the model decides the sequence of tool calls at runtime, only when the task is genuinely open-ended and the path cannot be known ahead of time, such as debugging code where the needed steps depend on what errors surface. The trade-off is control versus flexibility: autonomy handles unpredictable tasks but sacrifices determinism and makes failures harder to trace, so you grant it deliberately and wrap it in guardrails like step limits and scoped tools. The default is the most structured pattern that can express the task.

followUps.question: Can these patterns be combined, and what does that look like?
followUps.answer: Yes, real systems almost always combine them, treating each pattern as a building block. A common composition is routing at the top to select a workflow, chaining within a chosen workflow to run ordered steps, parallelization inside a step to run independent subtasks concurrently, and an evaluator-optimizer loop around a step whose quality matters. An orchestrator-workers arrangement can itself use parallelization to run its delegated subtasks at once. The skill is decomposing a problem into pieces and applying the simplest suitable pattern to each piece rather than forcing the whole thing into one shape, while keeping the overall control flow as understandable as possible.

question: What is a LangGraph state graph, and how do nodes and edges work?
directAnswer: In LangGraph you model an agent as a state graph: a shared state object flows through a graph of nodes connected by edges. Each node is a function that receives the current state, does some work such as calling a model or a tool, and returns an update to the state. Edges define which node runs next, and conditional edges let a node's output decide the next node dynamically, which is how branching and loops are expressed. The graph has a defined entry point and can loop back on itself, so unlike a simple linear chain it can represent cyclic, branching agent behavior with explicit, inspectable control flow.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
A LangGraph app is built by defining a state schema, adding nodes, and wiring edges:
add a state (e.g. messages, current step)
add nodes (functions that update state)
add edges (fixed) and conditional edges (branch on state)
set an entry point, then compile the graph into a runnable.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Linear chains cannot naturally express loops, branching, or complex stateful agents, which is exactly what ReAct-style agents and multi-step workflows need. LangGraph exists to model these as an explicit graph, giving you fine-grained control over control flow, a durable place to keep state, and features like checkpoints and human-in-the-loop that a plain chain cannot offer.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You define a typed state, often including the message history. Each node function takes the state and returns a partial update, which LangGraph merges into the state, sometimes using reducers to control how updates combine, such as appending to a list. Edges determine transitions; a normal edge always goes to a fixed next node, while a conditional edge runs a routing function on the state to pick the next node, enabling branches and loops. Compiling the graph produces a runnable you can invoke or stream.

whyImportant: LangGraph is a leading framework for building controllable agents, so understanding its state-graph model is a common interview requirement. Knowing how nodes update shared state and how conditional edges create loops shows you can build agents beyond linear chains. It is also the basis for discussing checkpoints, streaming, and human-in-the-loop features.
realWorldExample: A ReAct agent in LangGraph is often just two nodes: an agent node that calls the model and a tools node that executes any tool the model requested. A conditional edge after the agent node checks whether the model produced a tool call; if so it routes to the tools node, which then loops back to the agent node, and if not it routes to the end. This compact graph cleanly expresses the reason-act loop with explicit, debuggable transitions.

nestedTopics.title: Shared state and reducers
nestedTopics.explanation: The state object is threaded through every node, and each node returns an update rather than mutating it directly. Reducers define how updates merge into existing state, for example appending new messages to the message list instead of replacing it, which is essential for accumulating history correctly.

nestedTopics.title: Nodes as units of work
nestedTopics.explanation: A node is a function from state to a state update, and it encapsulates one unit of work like a model call, a tool execution, or a decision. Keeping nodes focused makes the graph readable and lets you test, retry, or checkpoint at node boundaries.

nestedTopics.title: Conditional edges for branching and loops
nestedTopics.explanation: A conditional edge runs a function on the current state to choose the next node, which is how the graph branches to different handlers or loops back to repeat work. This is what turns a static pipeline into a dynamic agent capable of cycles and decisions.

followUps.question: How does a conditional edge enable an agent loop?
followUps.answer: A conditional edge attaches a routing function to a node that inspects the resulting state and returns the name of the next node to run. In an agent loop, the agent node calls the model and updates the state with its response; the conditional edge then checks whether that response contains a tool call. If it does, the function routes to the tools node, which executes the tool, updates the state with the observation, and connects by a normal edge back to the agent node, forming a cycle. If the response is a final answer, the routing function returns the end sentinel, breaking the loop. This is precisely how LangGraph expresses the reason-act cycle as an explicit, inspectable graph rather than an opaque loop, and the same mechanism supports arbitrary branching between specialized nodes.

followUps.question: Why use a state graph instead of just writing a while loop in code?
followUps.answer: A hand-written while loop works, but a state graph gives you several things for free that are hard to retrofit. Because the state and the transitions are declared explicitly, LangGraph can checkpoint the state after each node, so you can pause and resume a run, recover after a crash, or rewind to a previous step. It can stream intermediate outputs as nodes execute, insert human-in-the-loop breakpoints before sensitive nodes, and give you a clear, visualizable structure that is easier to debug than nested loop logic. The explicit graph also makes the control flow a first-class, testable artifact rather than tangled imperative code. For a trivial agent a loop is fine, but for stateful, resumable, human-supervised agents the graph's built-in capabilities justify the abstraction.

question: What is a router agent and how does the routing pattern work?
directAnswer: A router agent uses a first classification step to examine an input and decide which of several downstream paths, prompts, tools, or specialized agents should handle it. The routing pattern separates the decision of how to handle an input from the actual handling, so each specialized branch can be optimized for its own kind of task. It works by having a model, or sometimes a cheaper classifier, output a category, and the orchestration code then dispatches to the matching handler. This improves quality because a focused prompt for one category outperforms a single prompt trying to cover everything, and it keeps the system organized as new categories are added.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
Routing is classify-then-dispatch:
input -> router (which category?) -> handler for that category
For example, a support request routes to billing, technical, or account handlers, each with its own prompt and tools. The router only decides; the handler does the work.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A single prompt asked to handle many distinct kinds of input becomes bloated and mediocre at all of them, and optimizing it for one case can hurt another. Routing exists to separate concerns so each handler is specialized and independently improvable, and so you can send simple inputs to cheap models and hard ones to capable models, controlling cost and quality.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The router step is usually a model call, or a lightweight classifier, that reads the input and returns a category label, ideally constrained to a fixed set. The orchestration layer maps that label to a handler and invokes it with the original input. Handlers can be different prompts, chains, tools, or entire sub-agents. A good router also has a fallback or default path for inputs it cannot confidently classify, and you validate that the returned label is one of the allowed options.

whyImportant: Routing is a core pattern in the agent catalog and a frequent interview topic because it demonstrates separation of concerns and cost control. Understanding it shows you can design systems that scale across many input types without a single unwieldy prompt. It also introduces important reliability concerns like handling misclassification and low-confidence inputs.
realWorldExample: A customer-service agent routes each message: billing questions go to a handler with access to the payments system, technical issues go to a handler with troubleshooting steps and a diagnostics tool, and simple FAQ questions go to a cheap model answering from a knowledge base. This routing means the expensive, powerful model and sensitive payment tools are only invoked when the category genuinely needs them, cutting cost while improving answers for each category.

nestedTopics.title: Classification as the routing step
nestedTopics.explanation: The router is essentially a classifier that maps an input to one of a fixed set of categories. Constraining its output to known labels, for example with an enum or structured output, makes dispatch reliable and prevents the router from inventing categories the system cannot handle.

nestedTopics.title: Specialized handlers
nestedTopics.explanation: Each route leads to a handler tuned for that category, whether a focused prompt, a chain, or a full sub-agent with its own tools. Specialization is the payoff of routing: handlers can be optimized and tested independently without a change to one degrading another.

nestedTopics.title: Fallbacks and misclassification
nestedTopics.explanation: Routers are imperfect, so a robust design includes a default or clarification path for low-confidence or unknown inputs. Handling misclassification gracefully, rather than forcing every input into a wrong bucket, is essential to production reliability.

followUps.question: How do you handle a router that misclassifies an input?
followUps.answer: You design for the fact that classification is never perfect. First, constrain the router's output to a known set of labels and include an explicit uncertain or other category so it can decline to force a bad match; route those to a clarification step that asks the user for more detail or to a capable general handler. Second, you can have the router return a confidence signal and treat low-confidence results as uncertain. Third, build handlers so that if a misrouted input arrives, the handler can detect it is out of scope and hand back or re-route rather than producing a confidently wrong answer. Finally, you monitor routing decisions against outcomes, use the misclassifications you observe to refine the router prompt or examples, and consider a cheap verification pass on the route for high-stakes categories. The theme is graceful degradation plus a feedback loop to improve accuracy over time.

followUps.question: How does routing help control cost and latency?
followUps.answer: Routing lets you match the expense of the handler to the difficulty of the input rather than paying top price for everything. Simple, common inputs can be routed to a small, fast, cheap model or even a canned response, while only the genuinely hard or high-stakes inputs go to a large, capable, slower model. Because the router itself can be a lightweight, inexpensive classification call, the added overhead is small relative to the savings from not running the biggest model on every request. This tiered approach reduces both average cost and average latency, since most traffic takes the cheap fast path, and it also limits exposure of sensitive or powerful tools to only the routes that actually need them.

question: How does reflection or self-critique improve an agent's output?
directAnswer: Reflection, also called self-critique, is a pattern where an agent evaluates its own output against criteria and then revises it, rather than accepting its first attempt. Typically a generator produces a candidate, an evaluator, which may be the same model with a critique prompt or a separate model, judges it and provides specific feedback, and the generator uses that feedback to produce a better version, looping until the output meets the bar or a limit is reached. It improves output because models often catch their own mistakes when explicitly asked to review, and iterative refinement can raise quality on tasks like writing, code, and reasoning where a single pass falls short.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
Reflection is a generate-critique-revise loop:
generate a draft -> critique it against criteria -> revise using the critique -> repeat until good enough
The critique step is the key addition; it asks the model to find flaws before finalizing, which is the evaluator-optimizer pattern applied for quality.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A model's first output is often not its best, especially on complex tasks, and asking it to self-assess surfaces errors it can then fix. Reflection exists to exploit this: separating generation from evaluation, and feeding concrete critique back, tends to produce measurably better results than a single pass, at the cost of extra calls.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The generator produces a candidate. The evaluator is prompted specifically to critique, checking the candidate against explicit criteria such as correctness, completeness, or style, and to return actionable feedback rather than a vague verdict. That feedback is appended to the generator's context, which produces a revised candidate. The loop continues until the evaluator judges the output acceptable or a maximum iteration count stops it, preventing endless refinement.

whyImportant: Reflection is a widely used technique to boost agent reliability, and interviewers ask about it to see whether you know how to raise quality beyond a single call. Understanding when critique helps, and its cost trade-off, shows practical judgment. It also connects to the evaluator-optimizer pattern and to safety, since a critique step can catch problematic outputs before they are returned.
realWorldExample: A coding agent writes a function, then runs a self-critique step that checks the code against the requirements and considers edge cases, and often against actual test results. The critique might note a missing null check; the generator revises to add it. Grounding the critique in real test output rather than the model's opinion is especially powerful, because failing tests give concrete, trustworthy feedback the model can act on to fix the code.

nestedTopics.title: Separating generation from evaluation
nestedTopics.explanation: Reflection works best when critique is a distinct step with its own prompt, or even a separate model, focused solely on finding flaws. Separating the roles keeps the evaluator from being anchored to the generator's choices and produces sharper, more useful feedback.

nestedTopics.title: Grounding the critique
nestedTopics.explanation: Critique is far more valuable when tied to objective signals, such as test results, a schema check, or a rubric, rather than the model's unaided opinion. Grounded feedback is trustworthy and actionable, which is why coding agents pair reflection with running tests.

nestedTopics.title: Iteration limits and diminishing returns
nestedTopics.explanation: Refinement usually helps most in the first one or two iterations and then plateaus or even regresses. A hard iteration cap prevents runaway cost and stops the loop once further critique stops improving the output, which is a necessary guardrail.

followUps.question: When is reflection worth the extra cost, and when is it not?
followUps.answer: Reflection is worth it when the task has clear evaluation criteria, when quality matters enough to justify extra calls, and when a first pass reliably leaves fixable errors, such as complex writing, code that can be tested, or multi-step reasoning where mistakes are common. It is especially worthwhile when you can ground the critique in objective signals like test results, because then the feedback is trustworthy. It is not worth it for simple tasks a model handles well in one pass, for latency-sensitive interactions where extra round-trips are unacceptable, or when the evaluation criteria are so vague that the critique cannot give actionable feedback and the model just churns. You should measure whether reflection actually improves your metric before adopting it, since it roughly doubles or more the cost per output.

followUps.question: Why is a separate evaluator sometimes better than self-critique by the same model?
followUps.answer: The same model critiquing its own output can be anchored to the choices it already made, sharing the same blind spots and biases that produced the flaw in the first place, so it may rate its work more favorably than warranted. A separate evaluator, whether a different model, a differently prompted instance, or an objective checker, approaches the output fresh and is less committed to defending it, so it tends to catch issues the generator missed. Using a distinct evaluator also lets you specialize it purely for judging against criteria, and using an objective evaluator like a test suite or schema validator removes model opinion entirely. The trade-off is added cost and complexity, so self-critique is a reasonable default and a separate evaluator is an upgrade for high-stakes quality where independent judgment clearly helps.

question: How does human-in-the-loop work in agent orchestration, and why is it needed?
directAnswer: Human-in-the-loop means pausing an agent at defined points so a person can review, approve, edit, or provide input before the agent proceeds. It is needed because fully autonomous agents can take costly, irreversible, or sensitive actions, and human oversight adds a safety and quality checkpoint where mistakes are expensive. In practice, the orchestration framework interrupts execution before a critical step, surfaces the proposed action and context to a human, and resumes only after the human responds. Frameworks like LangGraph support this directly through interrupts and durable checkpoints, so a run can pause indefinitely and continue later with the human's decision merged into state.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
Human-in-the-loop inserts a person into the loop at chosen points:
agent proposes action -> pause -> human reviews / approves / edits -> agent resumes
Common forms are approval before a sensitive action, editing an agent's draft, or answering a clarifying question the agent raises.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Autonomy is risky when actions have real consequences, such as spending money, sending communications, or modifying data, and models are not perfectly reliable. Human-in-the-loop exists to keep a person accountable at high-stakes moments, to catch errors before they cause harm, and to inject judgment the model lacks, trading some autonomy and speed for safety and trust.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The orchestrator marks certain nodes or steps as requiring human input and interrupts execution there, persisting the current state via a checkpoint so nothing is lost. The proposed action and relevant context are presented to a human through some interface. When the human approves, rejects, or edits, that decision is written back into the state and the graph resumes from the checkpoint. Because state is durable, the pause can last seconds or days without losing progress.

whyImportant: Human-in-the-loop is central to deploying agents safely in production, so interviewers probe it to see whether you design for oversight rather than blind autonomy. Understanding how to pause, persist state, and resume shows you can build trustworthy systems. It also ties directly to checkpoints and to deciding which actions are risky enough to gate.
realWorldExample: A financial-operations agent can draft and prepare a payment but is configured to pause before actually sending money above a threshold. It presents the payee, amount, and reasoning to an operator, who approves or rejects. Only on approval does the agent execute the transfer. This gates the one irreversible, high-stakes action behind a human while letting the agent automate everything leading up to it.

nestedTopics.title: Approval gates before risky actions
nestedTopics.explanation: The most common form is an approval checkpoint before an action that is irreversible, costly, or sensitive. The agent proposes, a human approves or vetoes, and only approved actions execute, which contains the blast radius of a mistaken agent decision.

nestedTopics.title: Editing and steering
nestedTopics.explanation: Beyond yes-or-no approval, humans can edit an agent's proposed output or state, for example correcting a draft or adjusting a plan, before letting it continue. This blends human judgment with agent throughput and is useful when the agent is mostly right but needs supervision.

nestedTopics.title: Durable pause and resume
nestedTopics.explanation: Because the framework checkpoints state when it interrupts, a run can wait for human input for an arbitrary time and resume exactly where it left off. Durability is what makes human-in-the-loop practical, since humans respond on their own schedule, not instantly.

followUps.question: How do checkpoints make human-in-the-loop reliable?
followUps.answer: A checkpoint is a persisted snapshot of the agent's full state at a point in the graph, saved to durable storage. When the agent hits a human-in-the-loop interrupt, it writes a checkpoint and stops, so the entire in-progress run, including message history and intermediate results, survives even if the process restarts or the human takes days to respond. When the human provides their decision, the framework loads the checkpoint, merges the input into state, and resumes from exactly that node rather than restarting from scratch. This durability is what lets a pause be indefinite and safe: no work is lost, no expensive earlier steps are re-run, and the resume is deterministic. Without checkpoints you would either have to keep the process alive the whole time or lose progress, both of which are impractical for real human review cycles.

followUps.question: How do you decide which steps should require human approval?
followUps.answer: You gate the steps whose consequences are hardest to undo or most costly if wrong, and let the rest run autonomously. The main factors are reversibility, since irreversible actions like sending money, deleting data, or emailing a customer deserve a gate while easily undone actions do not; the magnitude of impact, so large transactions or broad changes are gated while trivial ones are not; the model's confidence and the risk of the specific action; and any regulatory or policy requirement for human accountability. You also weigh the cost of the gate, because gating too much destroys the efficiency benefit of automation and trains reviewers to rubber-stamp. The goal is to place gates precisely at the high-stakes, hard-to-reverse moments and to let the agent handle the low-risk bulk of the work unsupervised, often using thresholds so only actions above a certain size or risk require approval.

question: What is LCEL and how does it help compose LangChain components?
directAnswer: LCEL, the LangChain Expression Language, is a declarative way to compose LangChain components into a pipeline using the pipe operator, so prompt | model | parser reads left to right as data flowing through stages. Every component implements a common Runnable interface, which is what lets them be chained, and the resulting composition is itself a Runnable with a uniform set of methods like invoke, batch, and stream. LCEL helps because it gives you streaming, batching, async execution, and parallelism largely for free, and it makes chains concise and readable. It is the idiomatic modern way to wire LangChain pieces together instead of manually calling each component.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
LCEL uses the pipe operator to connect Runnables:
chain = prompt | model | parser
result = chain.invoke({ 'topic': 'agents' })
The output of each stage becomes the input of the next. You can also run components in parallel by composing them into a map of Runnables.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Manually orchestrating prompt formatting, model calls, parsing, streaming, and batching for every chain is repetitive and error-prone. LCEL exists to make composition declarative and to bake in production concerns, so any LCEL chain automatically supports synchronous and async invocation, batching over many inputs, and token streaming without you writing that plumbing.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Because each component conforms to the Runnable interface, the pipe operator wires them so the previous stage's output feeds the next stage's input. The composed chain exposes invoke for a single input, batch for many, and stream for incremental output, and it can run branches in parallel when you compose Runnables into a parallel map. LCEL also propagates configuration and supports fallbacks and retries as part of the composition, so operational behavior is defined declaratively alongside the flow.

whyImportant: LCEL is the standard composition mechanism in modern LangChain, so interviewers expect you to recognize and use it. Understanding that the pipe operator relies on a shared Runnable interface, and that composition grants streaming and batching automatically, shows real familiarity. It also frames the discussion of how LangChain differs from lower-level graph frameworks.
realWorldExample: A summarization endpoint is built as an LCEL chain of a prompt template, a chat model, and a string parser. Because it is LCEL, the same chain serves single requests with invoke, processes a nightly batch of documents with batch, and streams tokens to the UI with stream, all without writing separate code paths. Swapping the model or adding a retriever stage is a one-line change to the pipeline, which keeps the code compact and maintainable.

nestedTopics.title: The Runnable interface
nestedTopics.explanation: Every LCEL-composable component is a Runnable with a common contract, including invoke, batch, and stream. This shared interface is the foundation that lets arbitrary components be piped together and lets the composed chain behave uniformly regardless of what it contains.

nestedTopics.title: Streaming, batching, and async for free
nestedTopics.explanation: Because operational behavior is defined by the Runnable interface, any LCEL chain automatically supports token streaming, efficient batching over many inputs, and async execution. You get these production capabilities without hand-writing them, which is a major reason to compose with LCEL.

nestedTopics.title: Parallel composition and fallbacks
nestedTopics.explanation: LCEL lets you run components in parallel by composing them into a map of Runnables whose outputs are gathered together, and it supports attaching fallbacks and retries declaratively. This makes it easy to fan out work and to build resilience directly into the pipeline definition.

followUps.question: How does LCEL relate to LangGraph, and when would you use each?
followUps.answer: LCEL is for composing components into pipelines whose flow is essentially linear or a simple directed acyclic graph, and it shines when data flows forward through stages with optional parallel branches, giving you streaming, batching, and async for free. LangGraph is for stateful agents whose control flow needs cycles, conditional branching, persistent checkpoints, and human-in-the-loop pauses, which LCEL's forward-flowing composition does not naturally express. You use LCEL for chains and retrieval-augmented pipelines, and LangGraph when you need loops like the reason-act cycle or durable, resumable, supervised agents. They are complementary: LCEL chains are frequently used as the work inside individual LangGraph nodes, so a node might run an LCEL prompt-model-parser pipeline while the graph handles the looping and state around it.

followUps.question: What does it mean that streaming comes for free with an LCEL chain?
followUps.answer: It means that because every stage implements the Runnable streaming contract, the composed chain can produce output incrementally without you writing any streaming logic. When you call stream on the chain, tokens from the model flow out as they are generated and pass through downstream stages that support streaming, so a UI can display partial results immediately instead of waiting for the whole response. The framework handles propagating chunks through the pipeline and merging partial outputs where needed. This matters for user experience in chat interfaces where perceived latency drops dramatically with streaming, and the value of LCEL is that you get this behavior by composing standard components rather than building a bespoke streaming pipeline, the same way you also get batch and async invocation from the same interface.
